newsitem.title: USA: U.S. rejects Libyan appeal as try to 'con' world.
newsitem.headline: U.S. rejects Libyan appeal as try to 'con' world.

text.p: The United States on Tuesday rejected Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi's appeal for two Libyan suspects in the Lockerbie Pan Am bombing to be tried in a neutral country.

The two suspects, sought by the United States and Britain for the Pan Am 103 bombing in 1988, have never been turned over by Libya to face charges in the blast that killed 259 people on the plane and 11 people on the ground at Lockerbie, Scotland.

In an advertisement in the New York Times on Sunday, the Libyan Mission to the United Nations said the United States should treat the Libyan suspects the way it treated Timothy McVeigh, whose trial for the 1995 Oklahoma City bombing was moved to Denver, Colorado, to ensure it would be fair.
McVeigh was convicted earlier this month of bombing the federal building in Oklahoma City.

"We think that the United States should deal with all cases on an equal basis, and accept moving the trial of the two Libyan suspects to a neutral country. For a fair and just trial cannot be guaranteed in either the U.S.A. or the U.K. where it would be surrounded by hostility and intimidation," the ad said.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry, asked about the Libyan ad, said Gaddafi was trying to circumvent U.N. Security Council sanctions placed on Libya after the bombing.

"From time to time, Muammar Gaddafi tries to wiggle his way out from underneath the effect of those sanctions resolutions and the requirements placed upon him by the Security Council -- and it's just not going to happen," McCurry said.
He said Gaddafi had a "grand public relations strategy" that was "an attempt to con the world community into thinking that he is trying to be cooperative when he's not."

"It is very clear what he has to do, and the United States again calls upon the government of Libya to release the two suspects so that they can be tried properly in either Scotland or the United States," McCurry said.
